titulo.texto: Petroglyph and Ceremonial Scraper of Hunter-Gatherers

frase_gancho.texto: A desert stone where someone left spirals and deer tracks.

puente_narrativo.texto: The same peoples who carved the rock buried their dead in very dry caves. Look for a bundle almost a meter tall, wrapped in woven blankets and tied with cords.

guion_corto.texto: This stone slab, about forty-five centimeters tall, comes from northern Mexico and bears engravings made by desert hunter-gatherers. You can see spirals, wavy lines, and deer tracks. They were made by striking the rock with a harder stone, until the dark layer on the surface was removed and the light color beneath showed through. Beside it lies a flint scraper, a tool for cleaning hides and working wood and bone. No one knows for certain what the drawings mean; it is thought they may have marked paths, water sources, or sacred places. The peoples who made them did not build cities, but they knew the desert inch by inch.

guion_largo.texto:
Until now you have seen pyramids, palaces, and tombs. But in Mexico there were also peoples without cities. For thousands of years, in the deserts of the north, small groups lived by moving with the seasons: at one time of year they went where the prickly pears ripened, at another to the mesquite trees, at another to the springs and the hunting grounds. They hardly planted crops at all. Their home was the entire territory.

The Mexica called the peoples of the north Chichimec, sometimes with contempt, as if they were people without culture. And yet, according to their own traditions, the Mexica came from there: from Aztlán, in the north, and from Chicomóztoc, the “place of the seven caves.” It is a curious paradox: they despised those whom they themselves said they descended from.

To live in the desert you have to know a great deal: which plant is good to eat and which one heals, how long the water in a ravine lasts, where the deer pass. That knowledge was not written down; it was taught by walking. Think about what it means to learn all of that without books: every grandfather was a library. Perhaps that is why each engraving mattered so much: it was one of the few places where some of that knowledge remained.

What do the drawings mean? Several ideas have been proposed: maps of paths and springs, marks of the passing of the seasons, signs of territory, traces of ceremonies. Spirals and wavy lines are repeated in rock art across half the world, and in Mexico they appear from the mountains of Coahuila to those of the Northwest. The deer tracks speak of hunting, but also of an animal that was sacred for some peoples of the north. You will see it again on the Upper Floor, when we reach the Wixárika, also called the Huichol.

The flint scraper reminds you of an astonishing continuity. Flint breaks into blades with very sharp edges, and with that edge the fat was removed from a deer hide to make it soft. The first settlers of the Americas, those of the Peopling Hall, worked stone in a similar way. In the north, that way of life lasted thousands of years, until the arrival of the Spaniards.

And it was a way of life that was very hard to conquer. When the Spaniards found silver in Zacatecas, in the mid-sixteenth century, the nomadic peoples of the north defended their territory for about forty years, in what is known as the Chichimec War. It was one of the longest resistances of the conquest, partly because there was no king or capital to take. To defeat a people like this, you have to defeat every family.

That is the lesson of this slab. Without cities, without metals, and without pyramids, these peoples knew how to read a landscape that seemed empty to others. And someone took the trouble to strike the stone, for hours, to leave on it something that would outlive them. What would you leave engraved on a rock, knowing that someone will look at it a thousand years from now?

texto.Culture: Aridoamerica / Tradition of the desert cultures (Great Chichimec)
texto.Period: Lithic Stage to Postclassic (8000 BC-1500 AD)
texto.Material: Volcanic stone (basalt); flint and chert worked by percussion and retouching
texto.Origin: Deserts and mountain ranges of northern Mexico (Coahuila, Durango, Chihuahua, Sonora and Baja California)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The peoples of the desert were simple nomads, with no knowledge or culture.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They knew the desert like no one else: which plants to eat, where there was water, and where game passed. They left engravings on stone and resisted the Spaniards for about forty years.
